questions.stem: What is a Logical Data Warehouse (LDW)?
options: A new storage technology that replaces physical warehouses
An architectural approach delivering a unified warehouse view without physically consolidating all data into one repository
A data warehouse modelled strictly in 3NF
A cube of pre-aggregated data
A department-level data mart
questions.explanation: An LDW is not a new storage technology but an architectural approach that integrates data virtually and presents distributed sources as a single, consistent analytical environment.

questions.stem: What is the backbone of a Logical Data Warehouse?
options: ETL pipelines
Tape archives
Data virtualization
OLAP cubes
Data scraping
questions.explanation: The backbone of an LDW is data virtualization: queries are federated across multiple systems and results are combined into a unified output.

questions.stem: How does a Logical Data Warehouse relate to modelling techniques such as Inmon's 3NF or Kimball's star and snowflake schemas?
options: It requires 3NF only
It requires star schemas only
It is modelling-agnostic; the distinction lies in the physical location of the data, not the modelling technique
It forbids dimensional modelling
It replaces modelling with schema-on-read
questions.explanation: An LDW can still support 3NF or dimensional approaches; the distinction from a physical warehouse is where the data lives, not how it is modelled.

questions.stem: What does pushdown processing mean in a Logical Data Warehouse?
options: Copying data down into a central repository before querying
Processing is pushed to the underlying engines so analytical workloads use their compute power
Moving old data to cheaper storage tiers
Compressing results before returning them
Delegating governance to source system owners
questions.explanation: Processing can be pushed down to the underlying engines, allowing analytical workloads to leverage the compute power of those systems, particularly distributed engines.

questions.stem: In practical terms, how does a Logical Data Warehouse present itself to users?
options: As a collection of separate source system logins
As a semantic and integration layer exposing curated views, so users experience a single warehouse
As a raw data lake
As a spreadsheet export
As a set of ETL job schedules
questions.explanation: The LDW acts as a semantic and integration layer that abstracts physical storage locations and exposes curated views, so users experience it as one warehouse.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a governance advantage of a well-implemented Logical Data Warehouse?
options: Metadata, lineage, access control and quality enforcement can be centralised through the logical layer
Governance becomes unnecessary because data is not moved
Each source system governs itself independently
Access control is delegated to the BI tool
History is preserved automatically
questions.explanation: Since all access is mediated through the logical layer, metadata management, lineage tracking, access control and quality enforcement can be standardised and consistently applied.

questions.stem: Why is a Logical Data Warehouse less suitable for regulatory reporting, auditing and long-term trend analysis?
options: Because it cannot run SQL
Because it does not inherently provide historical storage; if sources do not retain history, the LDW cannot reconstruct it
Because regulators forbid virtualization
Because it only supports unstructured data
Because it cannot integrate APIs
questions.explanation: An LDW does not inherently store history, so unless there is a separate historical repository it cannot reconstruct what source systems have not retained.

questions.stem: What risk arises when a Logical Data Warehouse pushes analytical queries down into operational (OLTP) systems?
options: Data becomes encrypted
Performance degradation, as operational workloads compete with analytical queries and service levels may be violated
Historical data is duplicated
The semantic layer stops working
Metadata is lost
questions.explanation: What is beneficial in analytical engines becomes a risk in transactional systems: operational workloads may compete with analytical queries, potentially causing service level violations.

questions.stem: Why does federated access in a Logical Data Warehouse raise security concerns?
options: Because all data must be decrypted in transit
Because it increases the surface area for misconfiguration and may expose sensitive datasets or create unintended access paths
Because passwords must be shared across systems
Because it disables access control lists
Because it stores copies of data in every source
questions.explanation: Federated access widens the surface area for potential misconfiguration, so strong security architecture and strict access management controls are essential.

questions.stem: How should a Logical Data Warehouse be positioned relative to a physical data warehouse?
options: As a full replacement for the physical warehouse
As an architectural complement, often in a hybrid where the physical warehouse holds curated history, a lake holds raw data, and the logical layer unifies access
As a temporary staging area before loading the physical warehouse
As a data mart for one department
As a backup of the physical warehouse
questions.explanation: An LDW is not a replacement but a complement; in mature enterprises a hybrid model uses the logical layer as the orchestration and semantic layer across warehouse and lake.
